title: Food & Cooking · Episode 1
chapters: Pots and pans: what your cookware is doing

units.t: Food & Cooking. Episode one.
In this episode: Knife skills, Pots and pans: what your cookware is doing, The science of flavour and Food safety at home.
Part one. Knife skills.
One good knife, used well, makes cooking faster, safer and far more enjoyable.
Choosing your knives.
You don't need a block of 15 knives.
A chef's knife, 20 to 25 centimetres long, does most of the chopping, slicing and dicing.
A paring knife, around 8 to 10 centimetres, handles peeling and hulling strawberries.
A serrated bread knife saws through crusty bread and ripe tomatoes without squashing them.
Hold a chef's knife before buying: it should feel balanced, with knuckle clearance above the board.
Western, especially German-style, knives use tougher steel and a thicker curved blade suited to rocking.
Japanese-style knives, such as the gyuto and santoku, use harder steel that holds a finer edge, often around 15 degrees per side versus roughly 20, but thin edges can chip on bones or frozen food.
Neither is better overall.
A mid-priced knife kept sharp beats an expensive neglected one.
Pinch and claw grips.
Most chefs use a pinch grip: thumb and the side of the index finger pinch the flat of the blade just in front of the handle, with the other three fingers around the handle.
This gives far more control than a pointing finger on top.
Stand square to the board and let the knife do the work, with a smooth forward or rocking motion rather than pushing straight down, which crushes food.
Your guiding hand uses the claw grip.
Curl your fingertips under, behind your knuckles, with the thumb tucked back.
The flat of the blade rests against your knuckles as a guide, and you walk the claw back as you cut.
It feels awkward at first, so practise slowly on a cucumber or carrot.
Professional chefs are fast because the motion is automatic, not because they rush.
The basic cuts.
Uniform pieces cook at the same rate, which is the main reason cuts matter.
Slicing means cutting across into even pieces.
Dicing means cutting into cubes: large, medium or small.
Mincing is chopping very finely, used for garlic, ginger and herbs.
Julienne is thin matchsticks, around 3 millimetres wide, and brunoise is tiny cubes cut from those matchsticks.
Chiffonade suits leafy herbs like basil: stack the leaves, roll them tightly and slice across to make fine ribbons.
To dice an onion, halve it through the root, peel, make horizontal and vertical cuts toward the root without cutting through it, then slice across.
Safe workspace.
Most knife injuries happen when something moves unexpectedly.
Put a damp tea towel or non-slip mat under your board.
Before cutting something round, like a potato, slice a thin piece off one side so it sits flat.
Use wooden or plastic boards; glass, marble and stone blunt knives and are slippery.
Keep a separate board for raw meat, or wash it thoroughly after use.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, because a blunt blade needs more force and is more likely to slip.
Wash knives by hand and dry them straight away; dishwashers dull edges.
Store knives in a block, on a magnetic strip or with guards.
Carry a knife point down, and if you drop one, step back and never try to catch it.
Honing and sharpening.
Honing and sharpening are different jobs.
A honing steel, the rod that often comes with knife sets, doesn't really sharpen.
It realigns an edge that has bent slightly with use, and a few light strokes before cooking keep a knife performing well.
Sharpening grinds away a little metal to form a fresh edge.
Whetstones give the best results: a medium grit around 1,000 for regular sharpening, and a finer stone of 3,000 or more for polishing.
Pull-through sharpeners are easier but can remove more metal.
Many kitchen shops offer sharpening services.
A simple test: a sharp knife slices a tomato skin cleanly without pressing.
The key idea: A chef's knife, paring knife and bread knife cover almost everything, and a well-kept knife matters more than a costly one.
Part two. Pots and pans: what your cookware is doing.
Cast iron, stainless steel, non-stick and copper each handle heat differently.
Know their personalities and your cooking gets easier overnight.
Spreading and holding heat.
A pan has two main heat jobs.
The first is conducting heat sideways from the burner, so the whole base is evenly hot instead of scorching in the middle with cool edges.
Metals vary hugely: copper conducts roughly twenty-five times better than stainless steel, and aluminium is not far behind copper.
The second job is storing heat.
A thick, heavy pan holds more energy, so when you drop in a cold steak the temperature does not crash and you still get a good sear.
Cast iron is a poor conductor but a great heat store.
No single material does everything perfectly, which is why cooks collect a few different pans for different tasks.
Cast iron and carbon steel.
Cast iron is heavy, nearly indestructible and can last for generations.
It heats slowly and unevenly, so preheat it gently for several minutes.
Once hot it holds heat beautifully, ideal for searing and frying.
Its seasoning is not grime.
When thin layers of oil are heated past their smoke point, the oil polymerises into a hard, slick coating bonded to the metal.
A popular myth says never to use detergent.
Modern dishwashing liquid is mild and will not strip well-polymerised seasoning, although soaking or a dishwasher can cause rust.
Dry the pan straight away and wipe on a little oil.
Carbon steel is close to cast iron in chemistry but rolled thinner, so it heats faster and is much lighter.
Woks and omelette pans are often carbon steel, and are seasoned too.
Stainless, copper and aluminium.
Stainless steel resists rust, does not react with acidic foods like tomato or wine, and can go from stovetop to oven.
On its own it conducts heat poorly, so good pans are clad, with aluminium or copper sandwiched between steel.
Food sticks when the pan is not hot enough, because proteins bond to the metal.
Flick in a drop of water: if it skitters as a bead, the pan is hot, thanks to the Leidenfrost effect, where a cushion of steam holds the droplet up.
Then add oil and food.
Copper is the most responsive metal, heating and cooling almost instantly, and is usually lined with tin or stainless steel because it reacts with some foods.
Plain aluminium is light, cheap and conductive but reacts with acidic foods and dents easily.
Hard-anodised aluminium is tougher.
Non-stick, and using it safely.
In 1938 the DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett was experimenting with refrigerant gases.
One cylinder seemed empty, but cut open it held a waxy white solid: the gas had polymerised into PTFE, a material so slippery and unreactive that almost nothing sticks to it.
In the 1950s the French engineer Marc Grégoire bonded PTFE to aluminium, reportedly at his wife Colette's suggestion, creating Tefal.
At ordinary temperatures PTFE is inert.
Above roughly 260 degrees Celsius it breaks down, releasing fumes that can cause flu-like symptoms in people and can kill pet birds.
An empty pan on high can get that hot within minutes, so cook on low to medium heat and replace badly scratched pans.
PFOA, a chemical once used to make PTFE, raised health and environmental concerns and has been phased out.
Induction and what to buy.
An induction cooktop does not heat a coil or flame.
A rapidly changing magnetic field makes electric currents flow inside the pan's base, so the pan itself becomes the heat source.
That works only with magnetic metals such as cast iron, carbon steel and many stainless steels.
Plain aluminium, copper and glass will not work without a magnetic base.
A quick test is whether a fridge magnet sticks firmly to the bottom.
When building a kitchen, a few good pieces usually beat a big boxed set.
A heavy frying pan in cast iron or carbon steel, a non-stick pan for eggs, a clad stainless saucepan and a big pot for stock and pasta cover most cooking.
The key idea: Good cookware spreads heat evenly and holds enough of it that cold food does not crash the pan's temperature.
Part three. The science of flavour.
Taste happens on your tongue, but flavour happens mostly in your nose.
Knowing the difference turns good cooks into great ones.
Taste versus flavour.
In everyday speech taste and flavour are interchangeable, but scientists separate them.
Taste is what receptors in the tongue and mouth detect: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.
Sweet signals energy, salty signals sodium and sour signals acidity.
Bitter may have evolved as a warning, though we learn to love it in coffee, dark chocolate and beer.
The old tongue map is a myth: every area with taste buds detects all five.
Fat is a candidate for a sixth taste, still debated.
Flavour is the bigger experience: taste plus aroma, texture, temperature and sensations like chilli burn or fizz.
Even sound counts, as people rate crisps as fresher when the crunch is louder.
Knowing which sense each element hits shows what a dish is missing.
Smell does the heavy lifting.
Your tongue reports a handful of tastes, but your nose tells apart a vast range of aromas.
As you chew, aroma travels from the back of your mouth up into your nasal cavity, called retronasal smell.
That's why food seems bland with a blocked nose.
Pinch yours while eating a jellybean and you notice only sweetness until you let go.
The claim that 80% of flavour is smell isn't precise, but smell supplies most of the variety.
The food pairing hypothesis says ingredients that share key aroma compounds go well together, like tomato and basil.
A 2011 analysis of about 56,000 recipes found Western cuisines often follow this, while East Asian cuisines, such as Korean, tend to avoid it.
Shared aromas create harmony; clashing ones create excitement.
Umami explained.
In 1908, Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda identified glutamate as the source of the deep savoury taste of kombu seaweed broth and named it umami, roughly 'pleasant savoury taste'.
It was accepted internationally as a basic taste after its receptors were found around 2000.
Glutamate is abundant in parmesan, ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce, fish sauce, anchovies and Vegemite.
Umami gets a big boost from synergy: combining glutamate with compounds in meat, fish and dried shiitake intensifies it far more than either alone.
MSG is purified glutamate.
Food regulators including FSANZ consider it safe, and controlled studies haven't confirmed 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'.
Chilli heat.
Chilli heat comes from capsaicin, which switches on a nerve receptor called TRPV1, whose normal job is detecting painful heat.
So the burn is a pain signal rather than a taste, and your body reacts as if your mouth were genuinely hot, with sweating, flushing and watering eyes.
American physiologist David Julius used capsaicin to track down that receptor, work that earned a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Menthol tricks cold-sensing nerves in a similar way, which is why mint feels cool.
Capsaicin dissolves in fat, so milk, yoghurt or coconut milk soothe a burning mouth better than water.
Birds barely feel capsaicin, so they eat chillies happily and spread the seeds.
Contrast and seasoning.
Cold dulls sweetness and aroma, which is why ice cream mix tastes cloyingly sweet when warm, and why chilled dishes like gazpacho need more seasoning.
Contrast matters too, because senses adapt to constant sensations: crunch on soft food, a sharp pickle beside rich meat, or salt flakes on caramel.
Season to taste means taste, adjust and taste again, at each stage.
Flat?
Add salt first, then acid.
Too salty?
Dilute with more unsalted base, or balance with acid, fat or a little sweetness; the idea that a potato draws out salt is largely a myth.
Too sour?
Add sweetness or fat.
Too sweet?
Add acid or salt.
Too bitter?
Salt, sweetness and fat help.
Too hot?
Add dairy, more base or a touch of sugar.
Adjust in small amounts.
The key idea: Taste is what receptors on the tongue detect, while flavour combines taste with smell, texture, temperature and more.
Part four. Food safety at home.
Australians get food poisoning millions of times a year, and much of it starts in home kitchens.
A few habits prevent most of it.
Bacteria and the danger zone.
Food Standards Australia New Zealand estimates Australians have around 4 to 5 million cases of food poisoning each year, with tens of thousands of hospitalisations.
Many are never diagnosed and are dismissed as a '24-hour bug'.
Causes include Campylobacter, Salmonella, Listeria, toxin-producing E.
coli and norovirus.
Pregnant women, babies, young children, older people and anyone with a weakened immune system face a higher risk, especially from soft cheeses, deli meats and raw eggs.
Most bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 60°C, the danger zone, and some can double every 20 minutes or so.
Keep the fridge at 5°C or below, ideally 3 to 4°C, the freezer at about minus 18°C, and hot food above 60°C.
Some bacteria make toxins that cooking doesn't destroy, so prevention matters more than reheating.
Time rules and leftovers.
The 2-hour/4-hour rule guides ready-to-eat food that has been left out.
It counts the total time between 5°C and 60°C.
Under 2 hours, use it or refrigerate it.
Between 2 and 4 hours, use it straight away.
Over 4 hours, throw it out.
On a hot Australian day, bring an esky with ice bricks to picnics and barbecues.
Leftovers are safe if handled well.
Refrigerate cooked food once it stops steaming, and divide large batches into shallow containers so they cool faster.
Eat within 2 to 3 days or freeze.
Reheat until steaming hot throughout, ideally 75°C, and only once.
Rice needs extra care: spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking and produce toxins if rice sits at room temperature, so cool and refrigerate it quickly.
Raw meat, heat and eggs.
Cross-contamination spreads bacteria from raw meat, poultry or seafood to food that won't be cooked again.
Store raw meat in sealed containers on the bottom shelf.
Use separate boards for raw meat and salads, or wash boards and knives in hot soapy water between uses, and wash your hands with soap for about 20 seconds.
Don't wash raw chicken: splashing spreads Campylobacter around the kitchen, and cooking kills it anyway.
Cook chicken, mince, sausages, burgers and rolled or stuffed meats to 75°C in the thickest part, because mincing and rolling mix surface bacteria inside.
A cheap meat thermometer removes guesswork.
Dishes with raw or lightly cooked eggs, such as homemade mayonnaise, aioli and eggnog, are a leading cause of Salmonella outbreaks in Australia.
Use pasteurised egg products and keep raw-egg sauces in the fridge for no more than a day.
Symptoms and getting help.
Food poisoning usually causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes fever, headache or aches.
Symptoms can start within a few hours of eating or take several days, depending on the cause; Listeria can take weeks.
That means the last meal you ate isn't always the culprit.
Most cases pass within a few days.
The main priority is fluids: sip water or oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy.
See a doctor if you have blood in your stool, signs of dehydration such as dizziness or very little urine, a high fever, or symptoms lasting more than a few days.
Seek help early if you are in a high-risk group.
Four everyday habits.
Most home food poisoning can be prevented with four habits.
Clean: wash hands before cooking and after handling raw meat, and keep benches, boards and tea towels clean.
Chill: refrigerate food promptly and check your fridge with a cheap thermometer.
Separate: keep raw and ready-to-eat foods apart.
Cook: cook high-risk foods thoroughly.
Also avoid cooking for others while you have vomiting or diarrhoea, and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Don't use cracked or dirty eggs.
When in doubt, throw it out: a smell test can't detect many harmful bacteria.
This is general information, not medical advice.
The key idea: Food poisoning is common in Australia, and bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 60°C.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the main trade-off of hard, thin Japanese-style knife edges?
Answer. They hold a finer edge but can chip.
Question two. Why does a heavy pan help when you add a cold steak?
Answer. It holds more heat, so it stays hot.
Question three. What is the difference between taste and flavour?
Answer. Taste is tongue-based; flavour adds smell and texture.
Question four. Why is the temperature range of 5°C to 60°C called the danger zone?
Answer. Bacteria multiply fastest in that range.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
